section.title: Righteousness Through Faith in Christ
section.sectionRationale: Paul warns sharply against those who would put confidence in the flesh and add law-keeping to the gospel. He lists his own unmatched religious credentials, then counts them all as loss, indeed as rubbish, for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ. This is the letter's clearest statement of justification: a righteousness not our own from the law but the righteousness from God that is through faith in Christ, whom Paul longs to know in the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings.
section.thesis: Against all confidence in the flesh, Paul counts his flawless religious pedigree as loss and rubbish compared to the surpassing worth of knowing Christ, so that he may be found in Him with a righteousness that is not his own from the law but the righteousness from God through faith, knowing Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the warning against confidence in the flesh; Paul's impeccable credentials counted as loss for Christ; and the righteousness from God through faith, and the surpassing worth of knowing Christ.

units.label: Warning against confidence in the flesh
units.note: the true circumcision worship by the Spirit

verses.text: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. It is no trouble for me to write the same things to you again, and it is a safeguard for you.
Watch out for those dogs, those workers of evil, those {{katatome|mutilators of the flesh}}!
For it is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh,

units.label: Credentials counted as loss
units.note: gain turned to loss for Christ

verses.text: though I myself could have such confidence. If anyone else thinks he has grounds for confidence in the flesh, I have more:
circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee;
as to zeal, persecuting the church; as to righteousness in the law, faultless.
But whatever was gain to me I count as {{zemia|loss}} for the sake of Christ.

units.label: The righteousness from God through faith

verses.text: More than that, I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have lost all things. I consider them {{skybala|rubbish}}, that I may gain Christ
and be found in Him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the {{dikaiosyne|righteousness}} from God on the basis of faith.
I want to {{ginosko|know}} Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to Him in His death,
and so, somehow, to attain to the resurrection from the dead.

katatome.gloss: A cutting down, a mutilation. Paul makes a stinging wordplay: the false teachers boast in peritome, circumcision, but Paul calls their work katatome, mere mutilation, a cutting of the flesh that counts for nothing before God. True circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit.

zemia.gloss: Loss, forfeit, damage, as of cargo thrown overboard in a storm. Paul takes everything the world would call gain, his pedigree and achievements, and moves it firmly into the loss column for the sake of Christ. What he once counted as profit he now reckons as debt.

skybala.gloss: Refuse, garbage, dung, what is thrown to the dogs. A deliberately crude word: Paul says his best religious achievements are rubbish compared to Christ. The point is not that his heritage was evil but that it is worthless as a ground of standing before God next to knowing Him.

dikaiosyne.gloss: Righteousness, right standing before God. Paul contrasts two kinds: his own righteousness from the law, which he renounces, and the righteousness from God received through faith in Christ. Justification is God's gift, a right standing credited to those who trust Christ, not earned by works of the law.

ginosko.gloss: To know, not merely to know about but to know personally, intimately, by experience. Paul's supreme desire is to know Christ Himself, to experience the power of His resurrection and even the fellowship of His sufferings. Saving faith issues in a growing, personal knowledge of the living Lord.

basic.context: Paul warns the church about teachers who insisted that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law to be right with God. If anyone could boast in such credentials, Paul says, it is him: born into the right family, trained as a Pharisee, faultless in law-keeping. Yet he throws it all away. Compared to knowing Christ, his religious resume is not just worthless but rubbish. What he wants is Christ, and a righteousness that is God's gift through faith, not his own achievement.
basic.hermeneutics: This is Paul's own testimony pressed into service against a false gospel. He uses his story to teach the heart of justification: right standing with God comes as a gift through faith in Christ, never by pedigree or performance. The passage is autobiography in the service of doctrine.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul mocks the false teachers' katatome, mutilation, over against true circumcision of the heart. All his gains he now counts as zemia, loss, even skybala, rubbish, for Christ. He renounces his own righteousness for the dikaiosyne, righteousness, that is from God through faith, longing to ginosko, personally know, Christ and the power of His resurrection.
basic.typology: Circumcision, the sign of the old covenant, finds its true meaning in the heart circumcised by the Spirit, as the prophets foretold. Paul's death to his own righteousness and life in Christ's fulfills the promise of a new covenant people justified by faith, the true Israel who worship by the Spirit.
basic.christ: Christ is the surpassing treasure for whom everything else is loss. Right standing with God is found only in Him, through faith, not the law. Paul longs to know Him, to share the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to His death in hope of resurrection. Christ is both the righteousness we receive and the person we long to know.
basic.god: God is the giver of righteousness. The right standing Paul craves does not come from the law but from God, credited to faith. God is the one worth losing all things to gain, and the source of the resurrection power Paul longs to experience. Salvation is God's gift, freely given, not a wage earned.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3 and 4 teach righteousness by faith apart from works. Galatians 2:16 says no one is justified by works of the law. Jeremiah 31 promises a new covenant written on the heart.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible moves from a righteousness sought through law and pedigree to the righteousness God gives freely in Christ. Paul, the model Pharisee, embodies the turn: everything the old system prized is loss beside knowing Christ, in whom God's long promise of a justified, Spirit-worshiping people comes true.

context.literary:
The chapter turns sharply at 3:1. Paul has been urging joy and unity, and then comes a blunt warning in verse 2 with three short stabs: dogs, workers of evil, mutilators. The change of tone is real, but the thread is the same, since the question underneath chapter 2 and chapter 3 alike is what the church trusts. Verse 3 states the thesis in three clauses, worshipping by the Spirit, glorying in Christ Jesus, and putting no confidence in the flesh. The rest of the passage unpacks those clauses.

Verses 4 to 6 are a list built for effect. It falls into two groups of four and three. The first four items were received at birth: circumcision on the eighth day, membership of Israel, the tribe of Benjamin, and the identity Hebrew of Hebrews. The last three were achieved: Pharisee, persecutor, and faultless under the law. What came by inheritance is set beside what was earned by effort, so that both sources of confidence are dismissed together.

Verses 7 to 11 then move into the language of the ledger. Paul has gain and loss, counting, and finally gaining Christ and being found in Him. The grammar shifts from the perfect tense in verse 7, 'I have counted', a settled decision made at conversion, to the present tense in verse 8, 'I count', a decision renewed daily. From verse 8 the sentence climbs through three purpose clauses, to gain Christ, to be found in Him, and to know Him, and ends in the hope of verse 11. The movement is from renunciation to possession to resurrection.
context.historical:
The people Paul calls dogs, workers of evil and mutilators are almost certainly itinerant teachers who insisted that Gentile believers accept circumcision and the law to belong to God's people, the same pressure that Galatians and Acts 15 describe. Whether they had arrived in Philippi or were only a threat Paul feared is unclear. Dog was a term of contempt, commonly aimed at outsiders, and Paul turns it back on those who relied on circumcision as a sharp piece of irony.

The credentials in verses 5 and 6 can be checked against what Paul says elsewhere. Circumcision on the eighth day meets Genesis 17:12, so he was born into the covenant and not a convert to it, as a proselyte would have been circumcised as an adult. Benjamin was the tribe of Israel's first king, whose name Paul shares as Saul, and it had remained loyal alongside Judah, 1 Kings 12:21. Hebrew of Hebrews most likely points to a family that kept the language and customs of Israel, 2 Corinthians 11:22. He had trained as a Pharisee, Acts 23:6, and says in Galatians 1:14 that he advanced beyond many of his contemporaries in zeal for the traditions of his fathers.

Zeal in the Judaism of his day was a prized virtue, and it carried the memory of Phinehas, who in Numbers 25:11 was commended for zeal when he acted to protect the covenant. Persecuting the church would therefore have counted as a credit and not a shame. That is exactly Paul's point: what once looked like the height of devotion is what he now puts in the loss column.
context.canonical:
Paul's argument depends on a pattern the Old Testament itself sets up. Circumcision was commanded in Genesis 17, but the law and the prophets already speak of a circumcision of the heart, Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6, and Jeremiah 4:4 calls on Judah to circumcise their hearts. Paul reads the covenant sign as a pointer, and in Romans 2:28 to 29 he says that real circumcision is inward, by the Spirit. Colossians 2:11 calls Christians' circumcision one made without hands.

The doctrine of righteousness by faith has its roots in Genesis 15:6, 'Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness', which Paul expounds in Romans 4. The prophets prepare the idea that righteousness would be given, Isaiah 53:11 saying the Servant will justify many, and Isaiah 61:10 speaking of a robe of righteousness. Jeremiah 23:6 gives the coming king the name The LORD Our Righteousness.

The New Testament develops the same thing in other letters. Galatians 2:16 and Romans 3:21 to 26 say that righteousness comes apart from the law yet is attested by it. Romans 10:3 to 4 explains how Israel missed it by seeking to establish their own. Second Corinthians 5:21 gives the exchange, that in Christ we become the righteousness of God. The goal in verses 10 and 11, to share His death and resurrection, matches Romans 6:3 to 5, Romans 8:17, and Colossians 1:24, where suffering and glory are linked as one path. Finally Jeremiah 9:23 to 24 stands behind the whole passage, where boasting is permitted only in knowing the LORD.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's immediate aim is protection. The Philippians are young in the faith, and they are being offered an apparently more complete version of it, with the marks of belonging to Israel added to faith. He answers not with abstract argument but with his own record. If any person could claim an advantage from the flesh, he could, and he walked away from it. That gives his warning a weight no theory could.

He also wants them to see what the real alternative is. It is not a different list of achievements but a person. Everything in verses 8 to 11 is ordered toward knowing Christ, and the righteousness he describes is given with Him and in Him. By setting out his hopes so openly, he lets them see that the Christian life is a wanting, as well as a believing: wanting more of Christ.

The passage also makes a pastoral move that is easy to miss. Paul does not despise what he had. He says it was gain. He is not mocking the law or Israel; he is saying that all of it, however good, was a lesser thing compared to the surpassing worth of Christ. The tone is of someone who found something so valuable that he could not keep holding the rest.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Paul's biography in verses 4 to 6 is description. It is not a recipe for how others must give things up in the same way or in the same order. The prescription is in verses 2 and 3: watch out for those who teach that the flesh gives confidence, and put no confidence in it yourselves. Verses 7 to 11 are testimony, but testimony meant to be copied in its direction, as 3:17 will make clear. Believers should reckon whatever they might lean on, whether heritage, effort, reputation or moral record, as loss beside Christ. That does not require abandoning a good upbringing or honest work. The point is that none of it can be the ground of acceptance with God. Be careful, too, with the language of rubbish. Paul uses it of his own claims as a basis for standing before God, and he does not use it of the Law, which he calls holy and good in Romans 7:12.

debates.question: Is the righteousness through faith in Christ our faith in Him or Christ's own faithfulness?

views.label: Faith in Christ received by the believer
views.case: The natural reading is that righteousness comes to those who trust Christ; Paul contrasts his own works-righteousness with a righteousness received through faith, credited by God to the believer.

views.label: The faithfulness of Christ
views.case: Some render the phrase the faithfulness of Christ, grounding righteousness in Christ's own faithful obedience; the BSB notes this alternative, and both readings exalt Christ as the sole basis.

debates.bearing: Either way righteousness is God's gift centered on Christ, received not achieved; the passage rules out any confidence in the flesh.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by so, somehow, to attain the resurrection from the dead?

views.label: Humble certainty, not doubt
views.case: The tentative wording expresses Paul's humility about the path of suffering, not uncertainty about the outcome, which the gospel guarantees to all who are in Christ.

views.label: Genuine uncertainty of final salvation
views.case: Read as doubt, it would clash with 1:6 and the whole letter's assurance; the somehow reflects the mystery of the road, not the security of the destination.

debates.bearing: The believer's resurrection is sure in Christ; Paul's language conveys reverent humility about sharing Christ's sufferings, not anxiety about being finally saved.

study.originalLanguages:
The three nouns of verses 2 and 3 form a deliberate play. Paul calls his opponents katatome, a cutting down or mutilation, and then says it is we who are the peritome, the circumcision. Both words come from the root for cutting. By using a coined contrast, Paul says the rite without the heart is no more than a mutilation, no longer a covenant sign. He sets the true people against the false with the verbs latreuo, to worship or serve, kauchaomai, to boast or glory, and pepoithesis, confidence.

In verses 7 and 8 the vocabulary is commercial. Kerdos is gain, and zemia is loss, a penalty or forfeiture. Paul uses the verb hegeomai, to consider or reckon, twice, and the tense changes: in verse 7 it is perfect, 'I have considered', a decision made once with continuing effect, and in verse 8 it is present, 'I consider', a decision still being made. The noun skybalon, rubbish, is a rough word for waste, refuse thrown out, a deliberately coarse term. The gain Paul seeks is of a different kind, kerdaino, to gain Christ.

Verse 9 says the righteousness is ek theou, from God, and the phrase dia pisteos Christou, through faith in Christ, carries a famous ambiguity. The Greek genitive can be read as faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ, and the BSB footnote records the second option. Paul then repeats the idea with epi te pistei, on the basis of faith, which makes the believer's own trust prominent in the verse. Whichever way the first phrase is read, the righteousness is a gift from God that rests on Christ.

In verse 10 the verb ginosko, to know, is the Hebrew idea of personal acquaintance and not mere information, as in John 17:3. The next clause lists power, dynamis, of the resurrection and fellowship, koinonia, of His sufferings. They are two things Paul wants in the one knowing, and the pairing prepares verse 11. Paul adds symmorphizomenos, a present passive participle meaning being shaped together in form with His death; the related adjective symmorphos appears in Romans 8:29 and Philippians 3:21.

Verse 11 uses the unusual noun exanastasis, a resurrection out from among, with a double prefix, and the phrase ei pos, if somehow, which expresses humble hope about the route, not a doubt about the goal.

typology.fulfillment: Circumcision was the mark of Abraham's covenant, Genesis 17:10 to 12, and the law already spoke of the heart needing the same cut, Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6. In Christ the sign meets its meaning. Paul says Christians are the circumcision because they worship by the Spirit, verse 3, and Colossians 2:11 speaks of a circumcision not made with hands. The escalation is from a physical mark on males to a work of the Spirit in everyone who believes, Jew or Gentile. The type falls short as a sign because it can be received without the heart, which is why the prophets and Paul both insist the outward rite is not the point, Romans 2:28 to 29.

Genesis 15:6 records that Abram believed the LORD and it was credited to him as righteousness, and Paul reads that as the pattern for all believers, Romans 4:3 to 5. The righteousness of Philippians 3:9 is the same kind of gift, now with its ground made plain. In Abraham's case it looked forward to the promised seed; in Paul's it rests on the work of the One who came, 2 Corinthians 5:21. The type falls short only because Abraham's faith was in a promise not yet fulfilled, while believers now trust the person in whom the promise arrived.

Phinehas was praised in Numbers 25:11 for his zeal for God, and Jewish memory held it up as a model. Paul had the same zeal and expressed it by persecuting the church, verse 6. His story forms a negative parallel, showing how a godly pattern can be turned against the purposes it was meant to serve when zeal is not tied to the truth, as Romans 10:2 says of his people. In Christ zeal is redirected and cleansed, no longer directed at people but toward the gospel. The correspondence is partial: Paul does not say Phinehas was wrong, only that the zeal he himself practiced was misdirected.

typology.type: Sharing the death and resurrection of the Servant
typology.fulfillment: The Servant of Isaiah 53 suffers and is vindicated, and he justifies many, Isaiah 53:11. Paul longs to know the fellowship of Christ's sufferings and the power of His resurrection, verse 10, and so stands in the line of those who follow the Servant. The fulfilment is that Christ's death and rising are the ground of believers' own, Romans 6:3 to 5, so their suffering is joined to His in a way no earlier servant could achieve. The type falls short here because the sufferings of believers never atone; they are the road to the same glory, Romans 8:17.

study.christ:
The passage is built around Christ as a person to be known and gained, not as a doctrine to be defended. In verse 8 Paul calls Him 'Christ Jesus my Lord', and the personal pronoun gives the verse its warmth. He is worth more than every credential, and Paul uses the commercial language of loss and gain to say so. The whole structure of verses 7 to 11 repeats the pattern of the hymn in chapter 2: the one who had every status counts it as nothing for the sake of another. Paul follows Christ down in verse 8 so that he may be raised with Him in verse 11.

Christ is the source of the righteousness Paul longs for. The phrase 'found in Him' says that the believer's standing is in a place, in Christ Himself, and not on a ledger. That is the exchange of 2 Corinthians 5:21, where He who knew no sin was made sin so that we might become the righteousness of God, and of 1 Corinthians 1:30, where He becomes our righteousness. Romans 10:4 says Christ is the end of the law to bring righteousness to everyone who believes. The law is not abolished as holy teaching, but as a way of earning standing it is finished in Him.

The passage leads to Christ by the pattern of His death and rising. Paul wants to share His sufferings and be conformed to His death, because the path of the Lord is the path of His people, 2 Timothy 2:11 to 12 and 1 Peter 4:13. Yet the sharing is of a particular kind. Christ's death was redemptive and ours cannot be. We are united to it, Romans 6:5, and our own cost is the form that union takes. The resurrection is also the sure hope, 1 Corinthians 15:20, because He has gone first as firstfruits.

It is worth noticing what Paul does not say. He does not say that Christ gives him more moral power to keep the law in a better way. He says the righteousness he wants is not his own at all. That shows the heart of the gospel: Christ is not an assistant to our righteousness but its replacement, and this is why the surpassing worth of knowing Him is not reduced even when everything else is gone.
study.god:
The central statement about God in this passage is in verse 9: there is a righteousness that comes from God. It is not merely approved by Him; it originates with Him and is given. Paul sets it against 'my own righteousness from the law' and it is the old distinction between a status earned and a status granted. This is the same God who credited righteousness to Abram when he believed, Genesis 15:6, and who justifies the ungodly, Romans 4:5. A God who justifies the wicked is unlike any god earned by achievement, and Paul is glad to worship Him.

God is the one who is worth knowing. In Jeremiah 9:23 to 24 the LORD forbids boasting in wisdom, strength and wealth, and says the only boast permitted is in knowing Him. Philippians 3 is that verse lived out by a man who had every ground for boasting and gave it up. The knowledge God offers is relationship and not information, and John 17:3 calls it eternal life. That means the God of this passage is personal, near enough to be known, and generous enough to invite it.

He is also the God of the Spirit. Verse 3 says that worship is by the Spirit of God, and it is the Spirit who circumcises the heart. The Trinity is present without being named as such: worship in the Spirit, glory in Christ, righteousness from God. The same God who gives righteousness also gives the power of resurrection, verse 10. The One who raised Jesus from the dead is committed to raising those joined to Him, Romans 8:11.

The passage also reveals His justice in the way righteousness comes. God does not overlook sin or lower His standard; He gives a righteousness that rests on Christ, so that He is both just and the one who justifies, Romans 3:26. The law's claim is met in Christ and not set aside.

For worship, this means the proper response is not self-congratulation and not despair. If righteousness is a gift, the only fitting posture is thanks. If knowing God is the prize, the right desire is more of Him. Paul's language of wanting is the language of someone whose heart has been captured.

crossReferences.note: The command of circumcision on the eighth day. Paul's own 'circumcised on the eighth day' in verse 5 answers to this verse, so he is claiming a birthright inside the covenant. The point is that the sign was real and valued, and still could not supply what only God gives.

Circumcise your hearts. The law itself asks for an inward cut, which means Paul's talk of a true circumcision is not a late reinterpretation but an old demand. Deuteronomy 30:6 adds that the LORD will do it, which is the promise the Spirit fulfills.

A man is a Jew inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit. This is the same argument as Philippians 3:3, set out at more length, and shows that Paul held it consistently across letters.

Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness. This is the root of the phrase righteousness on the basis of faith in verse 9. Paul uses it in Romans 4 to show that faith has always been the way God gives righteousness.

Israel did not submit to God's righteousness because they sought to establish their own. This is a precise description of what Paul's 'my own righteousness' means, and it shows that the same choice faces anyone who prefers a record to a gift.

God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God. It explains how the righteousness from God can be received by those who are found in Christ: He took our place so that we could have His.

The wise, the strong and the wealthy are told not to boast, but to boast that they understand and know the LORD. Philippians 3 is a case study. Paul sets aside every ground for boasting and keeps only the knowledge of Christ.

Paul says he has been crucified with Christ and that Christ lives in him. This is Paul's own description of what being conformed to His death and found in Him looks like day by day, and it makes verse 10 more than a wish.

Paul speaks there of a circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands. It shows that for Paul the true circumcision is something Christ does at the beginning of the Christian life, not something added to faith.

Believers are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, on the condition that they suffer with Him in order to be glorified with Him. This is the same road as verses 10 and 11, from sharing His sufferings to sharing His glory, spoken as a promise.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world in which people were given everything and trusted the Giver, and the fall is the moment they began to trust something else. Ever since, religion in its various forms has searched for a way to earn what was meant to be received. Philippians 3 is one of the clearest places where that whole search is brought to its end. Paul's list of credentials is a map of everything humanity has tried: lineage, ritual, effort, and zeal. He lays it all down.

The answer to the search was already promised in the Old Testament. God made a covenant with Abraham and credited his faith as righteousness. He gave the law through Moses, which showed the holiness of God and the depth of human need. Through the prophets He promised a circumcision of the heart and a new covenant written inwardly, Jeremiah 31:33, with a Servant who would justify many. Each of these pointed beyond itself, and none of them was meant to be a substitute for the one it pointed to.

Christ is where they meet. He fulfills the law, is the Servant who justifies, and gives the Spirit who circumcises the heart. Paul's testimony shows what that arrival means for one person: the proud Pharisee became the apostle to the Gentiles. The church is now the people of the circumcision of the heart, a family drawn from every nation who worship in the Spirit, as Romans 2:29 and Galatians 3:28 to 29 say.

The story is still in motion. Paul says he wants to know Christ, to share His sufferings, and to attain the resurrection. The old creation in which the flesh was the measure has been replaced, 2 Corinthians 5:17, but the new creation is not yet complete. The goal of the whole story is the resurrection of the dead, when those who are found in Christ are raised, and righteousness will dwell where the old confidence in the flesh once stood, 2 Peter 3:13.

quiz.q: Why does Paul list his impressive religious credentials?

options.text: To show that even the best human righteousness is loss compared to knowing Christ.
options.note: Verses 4 to 8 pile up his credentials only to count them all as loss for Christ.

options.text: To prove he had earned his salvation.
options.note: He renounces this very thing; righteousness is God's gift, not earned.

options.text: To boast about his superiority over others.
options.note: He lists them precisely to renounce boasting in the flesh.

options.text: To encourage others to trust their own pedigree.
options.note: He warns against confidence in the flesh, the opposite of trusting pedigree.

quiz.q: What does Paul count his former gains as, compared to Christ?

options.text: Loss, indeed rubbish, for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ.
options.note: Verses 7 to 8 call them loss and rubbish next to knowing Christ.

options.text: Still valuable achievements worth keeping.
options.note: He moves them all into the loss column for Christ.

options.text: Slightly less important than before.
options.note: He calls them rubbish, not merely less important.

options.text: The true basis of his standing before God.
options.note: He renounces his own righteousness for the righteousness from God.

quiz.q: What two kinds of righteousness does Paul contrast in verse 9?

options.text: His own righteousness from the law, and the righteousness from God through faith.
options.note: Verse 9 sets self-made law-righteousness against God's gift received by faith.

options.text: A greater and a lesser righteousness both earned by works.
options.note: One is not earned at all; it is the righteousness from God through faith.

options.text: Jewish righteousness and Gentile righteousness.
options.note: The contrast is law-righteousness versus God's gift, not ethnicity.

options.text: There is no real contrast; they are the same.
options.note: Paul sharply distinguishes his own righteousness from God's gift.

quiz.q: What is Paul's deepest desire in this passage?

options.text: To know Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings.
options.note: Verse 10 states his consuming aim to know Christ personally.

options.text: To be admired for his religious achievements.
options.note: He counts those achievements as rubbish; his desire is Christ.

options.text: To avoid all suffering at any cost.
options.note: He longs even for the fellowship of Christ's sufferings.

options.text: To return to confidence in the flesh.
options.note: He renounces confidence in the flesh entirely.

quiz.q: How does a person receive the righteousness from God?

options.text: As a gift, through faith in Christ, not by works of the law.
options.note: Verse 9 grounds right standing in faith, not law-keeping.

options.text: By keeping the law faultlessly.
options.note: Paul was faultless in the law yet counts it loss; righteousness is by faith.

options.text: By being born into the right family.
options.note: His pedigree is exactly what he renounces as a basis.

options.text: By a mix of faith and personal merit.
options.note: It is the righteousness from God on the basis of faith, not merit.

questions: Paul counted his best achievements as loss for Christ. What are you tempted to lean on for your standing with God instead of Christ alone?
Righteousness comes as a gift through faith, not by performance. How would resting in a righteousness you did not earn change the way you relate to God?
Paul called his religious resume rubbish next to knowing Christ. Is there anything good in your life you are treasuring above Christ Himself?
Paul longed to know Christ personally, not just to know about Him. What would growing in personal knowledge of Christ look like for you this season?
Paul was willing to share in Christ's sufferings to know Him more. How does the hope of resurrection make that kind of fellowship with Christ worth it?

translationNotes.note: Mutilators of the flesh renders katatome, a deliberate pun on peritome, circumcision; Paul brands mere flesh-cutting as worthless mutilation before God.
Through faith in Christ renders the phrase the BSB footnotes as possibly through the faithfulness of Christ; both readings ground righteousness wholly in Christ, received not achieved.
